arXiv:2607.20597v1 [math.AC] 22 Jul 2026

On mappings with Jacobian oneThanks: The author is grateful to Professor Lev Birbrair for the helpful discussions

Zbigniew Jelonek Zbigniew Jelonek Instytut Matematyczny, Polska Akademia Nauk, Śniadeckich 8, 00-656 Warszawa, Poland
E-mail: najelone@cyf-kr.edu.pl
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We show that the set A⁡(n,d)A(n,d) of polynomial automorphisms F:ℂn→ℂnF:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} of degree at most dd and with J​a​c​(F)=1Jac(F)=1 is Zariski closed. In particular every irreducible component of the set A⁡(n,d)A(n,d) of polynomial mappings with Jacobian 11 is either composed with polynomial automorphisms or (generically) with counterexamples to the Jacobian Conjecture. Moreover every such component has dimension at least n2−1.n^{2}-1. In particular if the set X⁡(n,d)X(n,d) is irreducible, and n≥3,d≥6n\geq 3,d\geq 6, then a generic element of this set is a counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture.

Key words and phrases: 
Jacobian conjecture, real Jacobian conjecture, local polynomial diffeomorphism
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary: 14R15; Secondary: 14P99.

1. Introduction

Nowdays there is a lot of interests in a counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture. Here we try to explain how possible counterexamples are located in the variety X⁡(n,d)X(n,d) of all polynomial mappings of degree bounded by dd and with Jacobian 1.1. It was suggested already by Drużkowski and Rusek [1], [2], that the variety X⁡(n,d)X(n,d) of such polynomials mappings is not irreducible (in fact they have considered the special case of the variety of maps in the Drużkowski form). Here we prove that every component of this set is either consists with polynomial automorphisms, either generically it is composed wiith counterexamples to the Jacobian Conjecture. It does not mean that X⁡(n,d)X(n,d) is reducible, but if not, then a generic element of this set is a counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture, at least if n≥3,d≥6.n\geq 3,d\geq 6.

2. Main Result

Lemma 2.1.

The set A⁡(n,d)A(n,d) of polynomial automorphisms F:ℂn→ℂnF:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} of degree at most dd and with J​a​c​(F)=1Jac(F)=1 is Zariski closed.

Proof.

It is easy to see that the set A⁡(n,d)A(n,d) is a constructible subset of Ω⁡(n,d)≅ℂM\Omega(n,d)\cong\mathbb{C}^{M} (where Ω⁡(n,d)\Omega(n,d) is a space of all mappings F:ℂn→ℂnF:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} of degree at most dd). Indeed, consider the algebraic set

S={(F,G)∈Ω(n,d)×Ω(n,dn−1);F∘G=identity}.S=\{(F,G)\in\Omega(n,d)\times\Omega(n,d^{n-1});F\circ G=identity\}.

Then the projection π⁡(S)\pi(S) of SS on Ω⁡(n,d)\Omega(n,d) is a constructible set by Chevaley theorem. But A⁡(n,d)=π⁡(S)∩{F:J​a​c​(F)=1},A(n,d)=\pi(S)\cap\{F:Jac(F)=1\}, hence it is a constructible set.

Hence it is enough to prove that the set A⁡(n,d)A(n,d) is closed in the euclidian topology. Let fk∈A⁡(n,d)f_{k}\in A(n,d) and fk→F.f_{k}\to F. Hence F=(F1,…,Fn)F=(F_{1},...,F_{n}) is a polynomial mapping with J​a​c​(F)=1.Jac(F)=1. We can assume that fn​(0)=0.f_{n}(0)=0. Indeed, fk​(0)=bkf_{k}(0)=b_{k} and bk→b=F⁡(0).b_{k}\to b=F(0).

Now if we show that fk−bk→G∈A⁡(n,d)f_{k}-b_{k}\to G\in A(n,d), then also fk→G+b.f_{k}\to G+b. Now let fk​(1,…,1)=(wk,1,…,wk,n)=wk∈ℂn.f_{k}(1,...,1)=(w_{k,1},...,w_{k,n})=w_{k}\in\mathbb{C}^{n}. Hence wk→w=F⁡(1,…,1).w_{k}\to w=F(1,...,1). If gk=fk−1,g_{k}=f^{-1}_{k}, then gk​(wk)=(1,…,1).g_{k}(w_{k})=(1,...,1). Note that the family of all wkw_{k} is bounded. Now let gk=(Qk,1,…,Qk,n).g_{k}=(Q_{k,1},...,Q_{k,n}). It is well known that the algebraic degree of gkg_{k} is uniformly bounded by dn−1.d^{n-1}.

For a polynomial Q=∑aα​xα∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]Q=\sum a_{\alpha}x^{\alpha}\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1},...,x_{n}] let ‖Q‖=m​a​x​|aα|.||Q||=max|a_{\alpha}|. Let us denote Q~=Q/‖Q‖.\tilde{Q}=Q/||Q||. Since Qk,j​(wk)→1Q_{k,j}(w_{k})\to 1 and wkw_{k} is bounded, we have that there is an ϵ>0\epsilon>0, such that ‖Qk,j‖>ϵ||Q_{k,j}||>\epsilon for every k,j.k,j.

Now we have Qk,1​(fk,1,…,fk,n)=x1Q_{k,1}(f_{k,1},...,f_{k,n})=x_{1}. Consequently Q~k,1​(fk,1,…,fk,n)=a⁡(k)​x1\tilde{Q}_{k,1}(f_{k,1},...,f_{k,n})=a(k)x_{1}, where 0<a⁡(k)<1/ϵ0<a(k)<1/\epsilon. If we take a subsequence of Q~k,1\tilde{Q}_{k,1} we can assume that it converges to a polynomial Q1Q_{1} and one of its (fixed) coefficients has norm 11. Moreover we can assume that a⁡(k)a(k) also converges to aa. Let us note that a≠0,a\not=0, because otherwise Q1​(F1,…,Fn)=0Q_{1}(F_{1},...,F_{n})=0 and Q1Q_{1} is a non-constant polynomial.

This contradicts the fact that F1,…,FnF_{1},...,F_{n} are algebraically independent, as components of a mapping with Jacobian equal to 1.1. Hence finally (1/a)​Q1​(F1,…,Fn)=x1,(1/a)Q_{1}(F_{1},...,F_{n})=x_{1}, i.e., there is a polynomial Q1′Q^{\prime}_{1} such that Q1′​(F1,…,Fn)=x1.Q^{\prime}_{1}(F_{1},...,F_{n})=x_{1}. In the same way there are polynomials Q2′,…,Qn′Q^{\prime}_{2},...,Q^{\prime}_{n} such that Qj′​(F1,…,Fn)=xjQ^{\prime}_{j}(F_{1},...,F_{n})=x_{j} for j=2,…​n.j=2,...n. This means that F is an automorphism. ∎

Theorem 2.2.

Let X⁡(n,d)X(n,d) denotes the space (which is an affine algebraic variety) of polynomial mappings FF with J​a​c​(F)=1Jac(F)=1 and of degree bounded by d.d. Let YY be an irreducible component of this set. Then either YY consists of polynomial automorphisms, or a generic element of YY is a counterexample to Jacobian Conjecture. Moreover, dimY≥n2−1.\dim Y\geq n^{2}-1.

Proof.

Let YY be an irreducible component. Then either Y⊂A⁡(n,d)Y\subset A(n,d) or it contains a counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture. In the latter case since A⁡(n,d)A(n,d) is closed it means that A⁡(n,d)∩YA(n,d)\cap Y is a nowhere dense in Y.Y. Now denote by ℒ\mathcal{L} the set of linear automorphisms with the Jacobian 1.1. Take F∈YF\in Y, which is not contaned in any different component of X⁡(n,d).X(n,d). Then F∘ℒF\circ\mathcal{L} is an irreducible set which is contained in X⁡(n,d).X(n,d). Since it has a common point which belongs to YY and does not belong to any other component it means that F∘ℒ⊂Y.F\circ\mathcal{L}\subset Y. But dimF∘ℒ=n2−1.\dim F\circ\mathcal{L}=n^{2}-1. ∎

Corollary 2.3.

If the set X⁡(n,d)X(n,d) is irreducible, and n≥3,d≥6n\geq 3,d\geq 6, then a generic element of this set is a counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture.

Proof.

Indeed, due to [3] we know that X⁡(n,d)X(n,d) is not composed only with polynomial automorphisms. ∎

References

  • [2] Rusek, K. A geometric approach to Keller’s Jacobian conjecture, Math. Ann. 264, 315–320, (1983).
  • [3] Alpöge, L., Hello there the Jacobian conjecture is false, X post, July 20, 2026.
